lead: XML writes data as a tree of tags. One root element holds nested elements, and attributes sit inside opening tags. A DTD or an XML Schema is a contract: it lists which elements and attributes may appear, in what order, and how many times. The contract lets two systems exchange a catalogue or a purchase order without guessing the shape. A DTD checks structure only. An XML Schema also checks types, so a price can be forced to be a number. This chapter writes both contracts for one bookstore record and tests a rupee sign against them.
prereq: You need Unit 2 for tag and attribute syntax, and 3.7 for XML as an AJAX reply.

sections.h3: XML: a tree with strict syntax

blocks.text: XML (Extensible Markup Language) stores data as a tree of elements. An element is a pair of tags with content between them: <title>Web Tech</title>. The opening tag may carry attributes, written name="value" inside the tag: <book id="b1">. Attribute values need quotes. Elements nest, and exactly one element is the root. XML is case sensitive: <Title> and <title> are different names.
An element with no content can be written as a single self-closing tag, <price/>, which is the same as <price></price>. The DTD content model EMPTY describes exactly this element.

An XML file may start with <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>, which gives the version and character encoding. Comments are <!-- note -->. CDATA keeps text unparsed: <![CDATA[ a < b ]]>. Entities write reserved characters: the entity < writes a less-than sign and & writes an ampersand. A namespace declares a vocabulary: <b:book xmlns:b="urn:shop"> puts book in the b vocabulary, so two vocabularies do not clash.

A document is well-formed when it obeys these syntax rules: one root, matched tags, quoted attributes, no stray angle bracket. Well-formed is a syntax test. Valid is stronger: the document also follows a DTD or XML Schema that says which elements and attributes may appear, and in what order. HTML is a fixed tag language with forgiving parsing; XML lets you invent tags and demands strict parsing. Browsers parse XML with DOMParser, and AJAX replies appear as responseXML; see 3.7.

A DTD (Document Type Definition) is a grammar for XML. <!DOCTYPE bookstore SYSTEM "bookstore.dtd"> attaches an external DTD. <!ELEMENT bookstore (book+)> says bookstore contains one or more book elements. <!ELEMENT book (title, price)> says each book holds title then price, in that order. <!ELEMENT title (#PCDATA)> says title holds parsed character data, meaning plain text. EMPTY allows no content; ANY allows anything.

Occurrence symbols control counts: ? means zero or one, * zero or more, + one or more. No symbol means exactly once. <!ATTLIST book id ID #REQUIRED> declares id on book; ID means a unique name and #REQUIRED means it must be present. #IMPLIED means optional. A default value such as status CDATA "available" fills the attribute when it is missing.

A DTD sees every element value as text. In <!ELEMENT price (#PCDATA)>, the contents 350, ₹350 and abc are all character data. The DTD cannot say price must be a number, cannot check a date format, and cannot give a range. It checks structure only.

sections.h3: XSD: a schema with data types

blocks.text: XML Schema, usually called XSD (XML Schema Definition), is a grammar written in XML. It adds data types. The root is <xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema">. <xs:element name="bookstore"> starts a declaration; its <xs:complexType> holds child elements and <xs:sequence> fixes their order. <xs:element name="book" minOccurs="1" maxOccurs="unbounded"> allows one or more books; unbounded means no upper limit. Inside book, <xs:element name="title" type="xs:string"/> and <xs:element name="price" type="xs:integer"/> declare the children. <xs:attribute name="id" type="xs:ID" use="required"/> declares the attribute.

Built-in types include xs:string for text, xs:integer for whole numbers, xs:decimal for decimal numbers with or without a decimal point (350 and 350.50 are both valid xs:decimal values), and xs:date for YYYY-MM-DD dates. A simple type with a restriction narrows a built-in type: <xs:simpleType name="priceType"><xs:restriction base="xs:decimal"><xs:minInclusive value="0"/></xs:restriction></xs:simpleType> forbids negative prices. The element then uses type="priceType".

An XSD parser knows price has type xs:integer. It converts the text and tests the integer rules, so ₹350 fails. A DTD has no type slot; it only tests that text is present. That is why XSD can type-check and a DTD cannot.

figure.caption: One record goes through the chapter's three checks in order: well-formed, then DTD, then XSD. Both 350 and ₹350 clear the first two, but the XSD gate reads price as xs:integer, so ₹350 is rejected.

examples.question: An online bookstore sends one record: title "Web Tech", price 350, id "b1". (a) Write the XML. (b) Write a DTD that allows one or more books, each with a required title followed by a price, and a required unique id attribute. (c) Write an XSD fragment that forces price to be xs:integer. (d) Is <price>₹350</price> valid? Answer for well-formedness, DTD validity and XSD validity.
steps: XML: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <bookstore> <book id="b1"> <title>Web Tech</title> <price>350</price> </book> </bookstore>. The root is bookstore; it holds one book element, which holds title then price.

DTD: <!ELEMENT bookstore (book+)> <!ELEMENT book (title, price)> <!ELEMENT title (#PCDATA)> <!ELEMENT price (#PCDATA)> <!ATTLIST book id ID #REQUIRED>. The plus sign allows one or more books; the comma forces title before price; ATTLIST makes id required and unique.

XSD fragment: <xs:element name="bookstore"><xs:complexType><xs:sequence><xs:element name="book" minOccurs="1" maxOccurs="unbounded"><xs:complexType><xs:sequence><xs:element name="title" type="xs:string"/><xs:element name="price" type="xs:integer"/></xs:sequence><xs:attribute name="id" type="xs:ID" use="required"/></xs:complexType></xs:element></xs:sequence></xs:complexType></xs:element>. The price element is forced to xs:integer.

Test <price>₹350</price>. Well-formed: yes, with UTF-8 the rupee sign is an ordinary character and the tags match. DTD validity: yes, because price is #PCDATA and any text passes. XSD validity: no, because xs:integer allows an optional sign and digits only; ₹ is not a digit, so the value fails the integer type.
examples.answer: The record is well-formed and DTD-valid but not XSD-valid: ₹350 is not an xs:integer.

traps: Well-formed and valid are not the same thing. A document with no DTD or schema can be well-formed but cannot be valid.
XML allows exactly one root element. Two top-level elements make the document not well-formed, so validity never gets tested.
A DTD treats every element value as text. It accepts <price>abc</price> and <price>₹350</price>; only an XSD type such as xs:integer rejects them.
XML is case sensitive. A DTD that declares price does not accept Price.
#REQUIRED makes a missing attribute an error. A default value does the opposite: it fills an attribute that is missing.

quiz.q: In a DTD, what does #PCDATA mean?
quiz.a: Parsed character data: the element may contain text, not child elements.

quiz.q: State the difference between well-formed and valid XML.
quiz.a: Well-formed means the syntax rules are obeyed: one root, matched tags, quoted attributes. Valid means the document also follows a DTD or XML Schema grammar.

quiz.q: Given <!ELEMENT bookstore (book*)>, how many book elements may a bookstore contain?
quiz.a: Zero or more; the star means zero or more.

quiz.q: A document has two <bookstore> root elements and a matching DTD. Is it well-formed? Is it valid?
quiz.a: Not well-formed, because XML allows exactly one root element. A non-well-formed document cannot be valid, because validity is tested only after well-formedness.

quiz.q: Name two XSD built-in types and the value each holds.
quiz.a: xs:string holds text; xs:integer holds a whole number. xs:decimal and xs:date are other built-ins.

quiz.q: Write a DTD attribute declaration that makes id required on book.
quiz.a: <!ATTLIST book id ID #REQUIRED>. ID makes the value a unique name and #REQUIRED makes the attribute compulsory.

beyond: Not for the exam. Relax NG and Schematron are alternative schema languages: Relax NG is compact, Schematron writes rules as XPath assertions. XSD 1.1 added assertions and conditional type assignment. JSON Schema does for JSON what XSD does for XML, and it is common in REST APIs. Industry vocabularies such as UBL for invoices and SOAP web services rely on XSD. Search for "XSD 1.1 assertion", "Relax NG compact syntax" and "JSON Schema validation".
